probes.query: An operator switches on write throttling for span storage. When the Elasticsearch cluster answers a bulk write with an HTTP 429 status, which chain of code classifies that failure as a capacity problem and reports it to the concurrency limiter? Start from where the throttling setting is read.
expectedFacts: ConditionalOnThrottledStorage.ThrottledStorageCondition matches only when the property zipkin.storage.throttle.enabled is true; it guards ZipkinConfiguration.ThrottledStorageComponentEnhancer.

ThrottledStorageComponentEnhancer.postProcessAfterInitialization (ZipkinConfiguration.java) replaces each StorageComponent bean with a ThrottledStorageComponent built from the min concurrency, max concurrency and max queue size properties.
ThrottledStorageComponent.spanConsumer returns a ThrottledSpanConsumer whose accept wraps the delegate's write call in a ThrottledCall (executor + limiter).
BulkCallBuilder.CHECK_FOR_ERRORS (the bulk response converter) throws RejectedExecutionException when the response status is 429, and a plain RuntimeException for other bulk errors.

ThrottledCall.EnqueueAndAwait.onError asks the isOverCapacity predicate (bound to the StorageComponent's isOverCapacity); ElasticsearchStorage.isOverCapacity returns true for RejectedExecutionException or ResponseTimeoutException, so the limiter listener gets onDropped (and requestsDropped is counted); otherwise onIgnore.
The limiter's new limit reaches the worker pool through limit.notifyOnChange(new ThreadPoolExecutorResizer(executor)) registered in the ThrottledStorageComponent constructor.
probes.author: r3h-zipkin-drafter
probes.notes: VERIFICATION: ConditionalOnThrottledStorage.java:21-31 (property check); ZipkinConfiguration.java:47-77 (@ConditionalOnThrottledStorage on ThrottledStorageComponentEnhancer, new ThrottledStorageComponent at :64); ThrottledStorageComponent.java:73-80 (Gradient2Limit + NonLimitingLimiter), :107 (notifyOnChange resizer), :120-122 (spanConsumer), :152-157 (ThrottledCall wrap), :175-204 (ThreadPoolExecutorResizer); ThrottledCall.java:163-179 (onError: isOverCapacity.test -> onDropped else onIgnore); ElasticsearchStorage.java:275-277; BulkCallBuilder.java:46-71 (429 -> RejectedExecutionException at :57-58). DECOYS: StorageComponent.isOverCapacity default (StorageComponent.java:90), ForwardingStorageComponent.isOverCapacity delegate (:56), CassandraStorage.isOverCapacity (:177) / ResultSetFutureCall.isOverCapacity (:116), HttpCall.sendRequest (HttpCall.java:188-197 wraps UnprocessedRequestException into RejectedExecutionException), ThrottledCall.STORAGE_THROTTLE_MAX_CONCURRENCY. Verified by reading every cited line.

probes.query: A producer puts one legacy Thrift-encoded span (a single span, not a list) on the Kafka topic. Trace the code from the consumer poll to the Elasticsearch bulk request, including how the daily index is chosen when that span has no start timestamp.
expectedFacts: KafkaCollectorWorker.run: when the first byte is <= 16, is not 12 (thrift list) and the payload is not protobuf3, the bytes are decoded as ONE span with SpanBytesDecoder.THRIFT.decodeOne and passed to collector.accept(List.of(span), NOOP); a decode failure increments messages-dropped.

Collector.accept(spans, callback) uses Runnable::run as executor: it samples spans (CollectorSampler via sample()), then runs StoreSpans on the polling thread, which calls storage.spanConsumer().accept(spans).enqueue(...).
ElasticsearchSpanConsumer.indexSpans chooses the index timestamp as span timestamp/1000 if set, else the first annotation's timestamp/1000, else System.currentTimeMillis().
BulkSpanIndexer.add calls IndexNameFormatter.formatTypeAndTimestampForInsert: index prefix + version-specific type delimiter + "span" + "-" + UTC date (for example zipkin-span-2024-05-01).
BulkCallBuilder.build turns all indexed spans of the batch into one POST /_bulk call (adding pipeline and refresh=wait_for parameters when configured).

probes.query: On the MySQL backend, an operator asks for the service dependency graph, but nobody has ever loaded precomputed dependency rows. Trace how the answer is produced on the fly from the raw span rows.
expectedFacts: ZipkinQueryApiV2.getDependencies passes endTs and the lookback (default from configuration) to storage.spanStore().getDependencies and encodes the links with DependencyLinkBytesEncoder.JSON_V1.

MySQL Schema's constructor sets hasPreAggregatedDependencies via HasPreAggregatedDependencies.test, true only when zipkin_dependencies has more than zero rows (a missing table logs a warning and gives false); the Schema is created lazily once in MySQLStorage.schema(), so the result is cached for the process.
MySQLSpanStore.getDependencies falls back to AggregateDependencies over the microsecond range [endTs-lookback, endTs] when nothing is pre-aggregated (SelectDependencies by epoch days otherwise).

AggregateDependencies first selects the distinct trace IDs with start_ts in range (so whole traces are read), then left-joins zipkin_annotations limited to keys lc, cs, ca, sr, sa, ma, mr, ms and error, grouped per span and streamed with fetchLazy.

DependencyLinkV2SpanIterator.ByTraceId groups rows per trace and turns each span's rows into a v2 Span (sr -> SERVER with ca as remote, sa/cs -> CLIENT, mr/ms -> CONSUMER/PRODUCER, an 'error' string annotation -> error tag).
AggregateDependencies feeds each trace to DependencyLinker.putTrace and returns linker.link().

probes.query: An operator on Elasticsearch lists the tag names whose values the web UI should offer as suggestions, with a repeat-suppression window. Trace how a tag value on an incoming span becomes a suggestion document, how repeats are suppressed, and what happens to that suppression when the bulk write fails.
expectedFacts: ZipkinElasticsearchStorageConfiguration.storage injects zipkin.storage.autocomplete-keys, autocomplete-ttl (default 3600000 ms) and autocomplete-cardinality (default 20000) into the ElasticsearchStorage builder.

The ElasticsearchSpanConsumer constructor keeps the keys in a set and builds a DelayLimiter with that ttl and cardinality; indexSpans calls addAutocompleteValues only when search is enabled and the span has tags.

BulkSpanIndexer.addAutocompleteValues skips a tag when key length + value length + 1 exceeds 256, when the key is not in the configured key set, or when delayLimiter.shouldInvoke(context) is false; the context is AutocompleteContext(indexTimestamp, key, value), so equality includes the timestamp.
Accepted pairs are added to the bulk request as autocomplete-type documents via BulkIndexWriter.AUTOCOMPLETE: body {tagKey, tagValue} and document id key=value, in the daily autocomplete index.
BulkSpanIndexer.newCall wraps the bulk call in handleError; on failure it calls delayLimiter.invalidate for every pending context before passing the error on, so the pairs can be written again.

probes.query: The Elasticsearch username and password are kept in a file that the operator rewrites while the server is running. Trace how rotated credentials reach the outgoing Elasticsearch requests, and what happens when the file is bad at startup versus later.
expectedFacts: ZipkinElasticsearchStorageConfiguration.BasicAuthRequired (username and password both non-empty, or credentials-file non-empty) creates the BasicCredentials bean and the esBasicAuth Consumer<ClientOptionsBuilder>; DynamicRefreshRequired (credentials-file non-empty) additionally creates the scheduled executor bean.

dynamicCredentialsScheduledExecutorService loads the file once synchronously (an exception there aborts bean creation, so startup fails) and then schedules the loader at a fixed rate of credentials-refresh-interval seconds.

DynamicCredentialsFileLoader reads a properties file requiring non-empty zipkin.storage.elasticsearch.username and password keys and calls BasicCredentials.updateCredentials; its run() catches and logs exceptions, so the previous credentials stay in use after a later bad rewrite.
BasicCredentials keeps a volatile string "Basic " + base64(username:password) that is replaced on each update.

The esBasicAuth consumer is collected into HttpClientFactory's customizers and applied in configureOptionsExceptHttpLogging; BasicAuthInterceptor.execute adds the Authorization header from basicCredentials.getCredentials() to every request (the health-check client reuses the same options).

probes.query: On Cassandra, a user searches by service name, one tag condition and a minimum duration. Describe how the matching trace identifiers are found and combined, and how they become full traces.
expectedFacts: CassandraSpanStore.getTraces turns the tag condition into keys via CassandraUtil.annotationKeys ("key" or "key=value") and, per key, calls SelectTraceIdsFromSpan (annotation_query LIKE ?, plus l_service when a service name is given) with fetch size limit * indexFetchMultiplier.

Because a minimum duration is present, getTraces also adds newBucketedTraceIdCall, which builds SelectTraceIdsFromServiceSpan queries (one per day bucket) using the duration-range statement; durations are converted from microseconds to milliseconds and the max defaults to Long.MAX_VALUE.
With two calls the results are combined by IntersectKeySets (retainAll over the trace-id key sets) and are not sorted by timestamp (only the single-call path uses traceIdsSortedByDescTimestamp).

The id set is flat-mapped into SelectFromSpan.SelectSpansByTraceIds, which keeps at most request.limit() IDs, selects spans WHERE trace_id IN ... with a LIMIT of maxTraceCols, groups them by trace id and, when strict trace id is on, filters the traces again with FilterTraces (request.test).

expectedFacts: Kafka: KafkaBootstrapServersSet matches when zipkin.collector.kafka.bootstrap-servers is non-empty and the enabled property is not the literal "false".

probes.query: A span reaches storage with no start timestamp. For each of the four storage implementations (in-memory, Elasticsearch, Cassandra, MySQL), how does the write path treat time for that span, and how does that affect whether trace searches can find it?
expectedFacts: Elasticsearch: indexSpans picks the index from the first annotation's timestamp (or the current time) and BulkIndexWriter.addSearchFields writes no timestamp_millis when the span timestamp is zero, so time-ranged searches cannot match it.

Cassandra: accept uses guessTimestamp (first annotation with timestamp > 0, else 0) for the index timestamp and falls back to the current time for the ts_uuid; when the guess is 0 it skips the trace_by_service_span and remote-service index rows (service/span-name rows are still written) because search needs a timestamp.
MySQL: BatchInsertSpans sets start_ts only when the timestamp is non-zero and has no fallback; searches filter on start_ts BETWEEN, so such a span row is never returned by a search.

In-memory: doAccept keys the span at timestamp 0 (timestampAsLong()/1000), so it sorts as the oldest trace (first to be evicted) and falls outside lowTraceIdsInRange; it is still retrievable by trace ID.

probes.query: On Cassandra, when mixed 64-bit and 128-bit trace identifiers are tolerated (strict trace ID turned off), which pieces of the storage module write or read identifiers differently than in strict mode?
expectedFacts: InsertSpan.Factory.newInput splits a 32-character trace ID into trace_id_high (first 16) and trace_id (last 16) only when strict trace ID is off.
InsertTraceByServiceSpan.Factory.newInput and InsertTraceByServiceRemoteService.Factory.newInput store only the lower 16 characters of a 32-character trace ID when strict is off.

SelectFromSpan.Factory.newCall(String) queries both the full 32-character ID and its lower 16 characters when strict is off, and newCall(Iterable) truncates each requested ID to 64 bits; with strict on, results are filtered client-side (StrictTraceId.filterSpans/filterTraces).

SelectFromSpan.SelectSpansByTraceIds only applies FilterTraces (request.test) when strictTraceId is on, because Cassandra always looks up by 64-bit ID.

probes.query: After a storage failure, can the broker redeliver the span message for each of the Kafka, RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ and Pulsar collectors, and what in the code decides that for each one?
expectedFacts: Common: Collector.accept calls callback.onSuccess right after scheduling the store, and a later storage failure only reaches StoreSpans.onError -> handleStorageError (spans dropped metric, debug log); the transport never sees it.
RabbitMQ: RabbitMQCollector.LazyInit.compute consumes with basicConsume(queue, true, ...), i.e. auto-ack, so the message is gone before storage runs.
ActiveMQ: ActiveMQSpanConsumer.registerInNewSession creates the session with Session.AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE.

Pulsar: ZipkinMessageListener.received calls acknowledgeAsync after collector.acceptSpans returns (before storage finishes) and negativeAcknowledge only if the listener itself throws (for example Collector.accept rethrowing a scheduling failure); decode errors are swallowed inside the collector.
Kafka: there is no commit or ack code; KafkaCollector.Builder only sets group id, auto.offset.reset=earliest and deserializers, leaving offset handling to consumer defaults or overrides.
probes.author: r3h-zipkin-drafter

DECOYS: KafkaCollectorWorker (poll loop only), ZipkinHttpCollector/Scribe (respond to caller, not a broker), ReporterMetricsAdapter.

probes.query: Where does the code cut time into whole UTC days for naming, partitioning or looking up stored data?
expectedFacts: IndexNameFormatter formats daily Elasticsearch index names from a UTC date (format / formatTypeAndTimestamp) and expands query ranges day by day, compressing whole months or day-decades into wildcards, from midnightUTC boundaries.
DateUtil.midnightUTC floors epoch millis to UTC midnight and DateUtil.epochDays lists the UTC day starts between (endTs - lookback) and endTs.
CassandraUtil.getDays maps DateUtil.epochDays into LocalDate values bound to the dependency table's day column.
MySQLSpanStore.getDependencies passes epochDays(endTs, lookback) to SelectDependencies (zipkin_dependencies DAY IN ...) when dependencies are pre-aggregated.
CassandraUtil.durationIndexBucket divides microseconds by a window (default 86400 s, overridable by a system property) to compute the bucket column of the trace_by_service_* tables.

probes.query: With write throttling enabled, which parameter limits how many pending storage writes may wait for a free worker thread, and what is the effective limit when the operator sets it to zero? What happens to a write that arrives when that limit is reached?
expectedFacts: The parameter is zipkin.storage.throttle.max-queue-size (STORAGE_THROTTLE_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE, default 1000), read by ZipkinStorageThrottleProperties and passed by ZipkinConfiguration to the ThrottledStorageComponent constructor.

ThrottledStorageComponent.createQueue builds a bounded LinkedBlockingQueue for the thread pool; a negative size throws, and zero is bumped to 1, so the effective limit is one queued write (despite the documented 'no buffering').
When pool threads and the queue are full, the executor's rejection handler throws the shared STORAGE_THROTTLE_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE RejectedExecutionException.
ThrottledCall.doEnqueue catches it, calls callback.onError, reports limiterListener.onIgnore (not a drop) because the executor, not storage, rejected, and rethrows so blocking callers see it.

probes.query: A user tags a span with a very long text value and later cannot find the trace by that tag in the search box, although the trace opens fine by its ID. Where do the different storage backends decide that such a tag is not searchable, and are the rules the same?
expectedFacts: Elasticsearch: BulkIndexWriter.addSearchFields skips a tag from the _q search field when key length + value length + 1 exceeds SHORT_STRING_LENGTH (256), and skips annotation values longer than 256.
Cassandra: CassandraUtil.annotationQuery skips a tag when only the VALUE is longer than 256 (the key length is not counted), and annotation values over 256, when building the annotation_query column.
The limit constant is RecyclableBuffers.SHORT_STRING_LENGTH = 256 (the Elasticsearch template separately uses its own 256 as ignore_above for dynamic string fields).
The trace stays retrievable by ID because the full tags remain in the stored span; only the index-side field is omitted. The two backends' rules differ (key+value+1 versus value only).

probes.query: On Cassandra, an operator finds that traces older than about three days still open by ID but never appear in the search results, even with a long lookback. Which code and schema settings cause this?
expectedFacts: The CassandraSpanStore constructor reads indexTtl as the default_time_to_live of the trace_by_service_span table through KeyspaceMetadataUtil.getDefaultTtl.

CassandraSpanStore.timestampRange computes oldestData = max(now - indexTtl*1000, 0) and clamps the start of the search window to max(endTs - lookback, oldestData), so searches never reach beyond the index TTL.
zipkin2-schema-indexes.cql sets default_time_to_live = 259200 (3 days) on the trace_by_service_span index tables, while zipkin2-schema.cql keeps the span table at 604800 (7 days).
That is why a trace younger than 7 days still opens by ID (span table) but is not found by search after 3 days (index tables expired).

DECOYS: CassandraUtil.durationIndexBucket (1 day buckets, not TTL), QUERY_LOOKBACK config (ZipkinQueryApiV2), InsertEntry TTL parameter (Cassandra v1 deprecated indexTtl).

probes.query: An operator blanks the character that separates year, month and day in the daily Elasticsearch index names, expecting names like zipkin-span-20240501. Follow how the blank value travels from the server configuration to the actual index names.

ZipkinElasticsearchStorageProperties.setDateSeparator rejects values that are longer than one character after trimming but stores the raw string, so an empty string is accepted.
ZipkinElasticsearchStorageProperties.toBuilder calls builder.dateSeparator(dateSeparator.isEmpty() ? 0 : dateSeparator.charAt(0)), converting empty to the NUL char 0.
IndexNameFormatter.Builder.build uses the pattern yyyyMMdd when the separator is 0, otherwise yyyy-MM-dd with '-' replaced by the separator, so names become zipkin-span-20240501.

probes.query: A message arrives on the Kafka topic. Under which conditions is it ignored, counted as dropped, decoded as a single legacy span, or handed to the general list decoder, and what happens in the list decoder when the first byte is unrecognised?
expectedFacts: Every record increments messages and bytes first; an empty value is then ignored without further counting.
A value shorter than 2 bytes increments messages-dropped and is skipped.

If the value is not protobuf3 (first byte 10 with a non-zero second byte), the first byte is <= 16 and not 12, it is decoded as a single span with THRIFT.decodeOne; a RuntimeException there counts a dropped message.

Everything else (protobuf3, a thrift list starting with 12, JSON starting with '[', or any other byte) goes to collector.acceptSpans(bytes, NOOP), which uses SpanBytesDecoderDetector.decoderForListMessage.
The detector accepts first bytes 12, 11, protobuf3 or '[' (JSON); otherwise it throws IllegalArgumentException, which Collector.handleDecodeError counts as a dropped message.

probes.query: With the server's self-tracing switched on, what decides whether a given incoming request starts a trace of the server itself? Cover how the sample-rate and traces-per-second settings interact and which requests are even considered.
expectedFacts: If sample-rate is not 1.0, the sampler is BoundarySampler for rates below 0.01 and Sampler.create(rate) otherwise, and traces-per-second is ignored.
If sample-rate is 1.0 and traces-per-second is non-zero, RateLimitingSampler.create(tracesPerSecond) is used (defaults 1.0 and 1 make the default one trace per second).
If sample-rate is 1.0 and traces-per-second is 0, Sampler.ALWAYS_SAMPLE keeps every considered trace.

The Tracing itself uses Sampler.NEVER_SAMPLE, so only HttpTracing's serverSampler can start traces: it consults the sampler only for request paths starting with /api or /zipkin/api and returns false for all other paths.
Consequently traces cannot start from other sources such as Kafka or Rabbit consumers (stated in the sampler's javadoc).

probes.query: In the MySQL backend, a client span and its server counterpart share one span ID and are written in separate batches, in either order. Whose start timestamp ends up in the stored row, and which rule in the write path produces that?
expectedFacts: The row key is (trace_id_high, trace_id, id), so both halves of the RPC target the same zipkin_spans row (primary key in mysql.sql).
BatchInsertSpans.apply sets START_TS in the INSERT whenever the span has a timestamp, even a shared (server) one, as a tentative value.

On duplicate key it updates START_TS only when the span is not shared, so the client's authoritative timestamp always wins regardless of arrival order, and a shared span arriving later does not overwrite it.
duration (non-zero) and parent_id (non-zero) are also written to the update set regardless of shared; name and remote service name only when not null and not "unknown" (updateName).

probes.query: Where does the server apply the storage throttle settings to trace search and trace lookup requests, so that reads are delayed or rejected when storage is under load?
expectedFacts: No code throttles reads: ThrottledStorageComponent extends ForwardingStorageComponent but overrides only spanConsumer() (plus close/toString), so spanStore(), traces(), serviceAndSpanNames() and autocompleteTags() are forwarded unmodified.
The throttle exists for writes only: ThrottledStorageComponent.ThrottledSpanConsumer.accept wraps the delegate's write call in a ThrottledCall (class javadoc: limits requests to the spanConsumer()).
The query API calls storage.spanStore()/traces()/serviceAndSpanNames() directly (ZipkinQueryApiV2), which resolve to the unthrottled delegates.
What exists for reads is a request timeout (zipkin.query.timeout, 11s) set in ZipkinHttpConfiguration, not a throttle.

probes.query: When self-tracing is on and Cassandra is the storage backend, where does each individual CQL statement execution become a child span of the request's trace?
expectedFacts: It does not: ZipkinCassandra3StorageConfiguration imports TracingSessionFactoryEnhancer (@ConditionalOnSelfTracing) but its postProcessAfterInitialization returns the bean unchanged; the wrapping with TracingSession is commented out.

The Cassandra driver instrumentation dependency (brave-instrumentation-cassandra-driver) is commented out in zipkin-server/pom.xml, and the zipkin-storage-cassandra module has no Brave code; DefaultSessionFactory builds untraced sessions.
What does get traced for Cassandra is the storage API level: TracingStorageComponent wraps accept-spans, get-traces and other calls in TracedCall spans for every backend.
By contrast MySQL gets statement-level spans (ZipkinSelfTracingMySQLStorageConfiguration's ExecuteListener) and Elasticsearch gets HTTP client spans (esTracing).
